utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I do understand that the preparation for the next witness to be called by the Prosecution give rise to some questions which the party would say like to discuss first before the witness will be called. Mr. Misetic, I think you were the one who raised the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. I rise because, as the Chamber is aware, yesterday the Gotovina Defence filed a witness statement of this witness which it formally took in July of this year. We filed it as a Rule 92 ter submission. In the e-mail in which I sent a courtesy copy to the parties and to the Chamber, I indicated that normally we would wait for cross-examination to put this type of statement to a witness. However, in light of Rule 92 ter and in order avoid a situation which actually came up with a witness a few weeks ago, which was Mr. Dzolic, whereby the witness makes 92 ter attestations when his statements are submitted by the Prosecution, and then in the Defence case, he makes corrections which he failed to make at the beginning, the Prosecution could, in theory, ask for Rule 91 instruction against its own witness. To avoid that situation, we decided that it was best if the Defence statement could be given to the Chamber and to the Prosecution so that in any proofing, as well as before the Rule 92 ter attestations are made, any changes that needed to be made to the initial statement given to the OTP, could be put to the witness and then the witness could make those changes if he deemed them necessary. If he disavows the statement given to the Defence that could also be put to the witness before he makes the Rule 92 ter attestation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that Ms. Mahindaratne could use this statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It was filed with the Registry, officially served on the Prosecution, and therefore, there was no reason whatsoever that the Prosecution couldn't use something that we had publicly filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Except, obviously, I should correct that the annex to the filing was confidential yesterday but, nevertheless, something the Prosecution could use. What transpired today is that the Prosecution didn't put the statement to the witness, didn't -- as far as I know, tell the witness that they are in possession of the second statement, proceeded to question the witness on matters that are in the statement without telling him, A, that they have the statement; or B, giving him an opportunity to review his statement to see if -- either to refresh his recollection, or, in my estimation, to alert the witness to the fact that there is nothing wrong with the fact that he gave a statement to the Defence, that we have filed it with the parties and with the Chamber, and that he has no reason to be nervous about the fact that he has given a statement to the Defence. Instead what transpired was, he has now been asked questions by Ms. Mahindaratne without the benefit of having seen the second statement. There are now inconsistencies between what he told Ms. Mahindaratne today and what he says in the statement he signed to the Defence. Inconsistencies, I would say, on peripheral matters which are, did he -- has he ever seen his statement to the OTP prior to today. Apparently he told Ms. Mahindaratne that today is the first time he saw it. In the Defence statement he actually says, I have now seen it today, and we go point by point through the statement. Now I think it was a disservice to the witness not to simply say we have received a statement, this is a second statement, please review it. Did you give the statement; was it coerced; did you freely give it; are these corrections that you made to the initial statement? So now we are in a position where the witness, not knowing that all the parties have the second statement, signed an additional statement today where he says that the first statement is accurate, but also notes that the statement he -- he acknowledges having given a statement to the Defence in which he says, But that statement was also consistent with what I have said in my first statement to the OTP. Now, I don't think that the Prosecution thinks that the statement he gave to the Defence in July is consistent with the statement he gave in January. So now we have a situation where the witness has not made substantive changes to his first statement in January but says that the second statement, in July he gave, is consistent with that first statement and he has never seen it because it was never shown to him. Now, from my perspective, from the perspective of the Defence, this trial is about a search for the truth. Why such a statement would not be shown to the witness is inexplicable to me. What purpose is served by not telling him that there's second statement out there that he should review before coming to court today and being asked to make the attestations in which he is swearing under oath about statements made in the first statement. I think it is unfair to the witness, it's unfair to the parties and it's unfair to the Chamber. I had a conversation with Ms. Mahindaratne where she said to me, that the reason she didn't show it to him is because, initially, she asked him, Is this the first time you've seen your statement. He said today is the first time he has seen his OTP statement. As a result of that, Ms. Mahindaratne concluded that the Defence engaged in questionable tactics to obtain the July 2008 statement, and therefore, there is no need to show him the statement at all because the statement is "defective." I think these are matters that should have been put to the witness, let the witness tell us if the statement is defective or not. They weren't put to him. I reject the allegation that the witness was manipulated, particularly where the Prosecution didn't put to the witness if he had been manipulated in any way, in the giving of the second statement, and particularly where the witness himself says that he thinks the second statement given to the Defence is consistent with the first statement given to OTP. So what we do now, I think I spoke with Mr. Waespi before we came to Court. We are both of the agreement that it will take the wisdom of the Bench to figure out how we proceed from here. I wanted to alert the Chamber to the situation, and to be fair to the witness, I think he should be allowed to see the second statement given to Defence. And I ask that he be instructed, because there is a common misperception among witnesses that it is somehow inappropriate to speak to the Defence, that he be told that if he gave a second statement to the Defence, that there's nothing wrong with that and that he shouldn't feel uncomfortable acknowledging that he gave a second statement to the Defence and reviewing it and telling us if what he said to the Defence is the truth as he understands it. And from there, I'm happy to proceed whatever the witness says about the OTP statement, the Defence statement and whatever other matters he is here to testify about. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think Mr. Misetic is avoiding the fundamental issue involved in this matter. First and foremost, I have to say we, the OTP, did not in any way make the witness feel uncomfortable about speaking to the Defence. In fact, in the supplementary statement, the witness has clearly admitted being interviewed by the Defence investigator. Now the issue was, Mr. President, I had the Defence statement with me at the time of proofing and I had all the intentions of showing the Defence statement to the witness. But when I questioned him as to whether he had been shown the OTP statement and whether he has made amendments or whether he indicated in any way that he wished to make amendments, he categorically stated that that was not the case. He has never seen the OTP statement and has never gone through the submissions or his statement point by point. Now, in the context of that position, if you view the Defence statement, it is clear that there is something terribly wrong because the Defence statement starts off by saying -- with the -- if I could take Your Honours to the first paragraph. It starts off -- paragraph 1 of Defence statement starts off in this manner: "I am giving a voluntary statement on my participation in the military police Operation Storm, as well as the events I personally participated in after Operation Storm. I must emphasise that I gave a statement to the ICTY OTP on 27 January 2008, which I haven't seen to this day. And on the basis of my notes which I had compiled during this interview, I sent a written amendments to my responses to the ICTY OTP." And then the second paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. In the second paragraph starts off in this manner: "I have been presented with my statement by persons from the office of the Defence of General Gotovina, and I can se that the amendments which, as I have previously mentioned, I sent to the ICTY OTP at the end of March 2008 have not been inserted into the statement." From that point onwards, the witness is -- the statement goes through point by point, he refers to paragraphs in the OTP statement and makes amendments. Now, yesterday the witness was very clear that he has never been -- he categorically stated and I repeatedly asked him the question, Were you given the OTP statement? He said, No, after I was interviewed by you on 27 January 2008, this is the first time I'm seeing the OTP statement. I never made any amendments. I never stated to the Defence investigator I wanted to make any amendments. He never asked me. I even asked him the Defence investigator had read back the OTP statement to him. He said no, that he was never shown any documents. In fact, this statement -- the Defence statement also includes paragraphs where the witness is shown documents and asked to comment. Now, in that context, it was clear to me what we had before us, Mr. President, was a problem. On the one hand, we have a statement filed by the Defence under 92 ter yesterday, which clearly is taken on the basis that the witness is given a statement and is making amendments to the OTP statement. And now, yesterday, the witness was denying that. So I believe that this was a situation that had to be dealt with and solved in the interest of transparency while all parties are present before Court. I did not think it was appropriate for me, in the context of what the witness told me yesterday and the OTP investigator, for me to go into the Defence statement and for me to try to divulge as whether it was correct or whether it wasn't. I believe that it should be done in Court in the presence of all parties. And I don't -- I don't understand why Mr. Misetic is so offended by the attempt -- attempt by the Prosecution to solve this matter before Court, in the presence of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to see whether I understood your position well. What are you saying that, in view of the answers given to your introductory questions to the witness, you were confused because there was so much inconsistency between what appears on paper as his July statement compared to what he told you yesterday, and for that reason you did not pay attention to the July statement, apart from that it was given and -- but did you not want to go into the content of it in view of the doubts you had on whether this would reflect what -- not only what he said but also what had happened on the 25th of July. Is that how I have to understand your position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. Apart from that -- because there is an issue about the methods which may have been used in obtaining the July statement, which I believed was a matter that should be sorted out before Court because to me, at that moment, it was clear that it was questionable, the methods of obtaining the statement and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When I use the words "what he said and what had happened," I on purpose avoided the words, methods or anything, rather to see to look at it in exclusively factual terms so that we not start or get already saying you're using method which is inappropriate, et cetera, et cetera. I would first concentrate on the facts what has happened. Anything else, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And apart from that, the Prosecution filed a 92 ter submission on 10th September. And the Gotovina Defence filed their objection on 7th October and not -- sorry, not objection, the response on 7th October, and in the response the Defence clearly stated that they had no objection to the submission. Now, on 7 October the Defence was in possession of this statement given by the witness in July. And clearly, at that stage, it was apparent if, in fact, the -- the statement that the Prosecution was filing by way of its 92 ter motion was, in fact, not accurate and has been changed subsequently, at that stage, the Defence should have, at the very least, alerted the Trial Chamber that in fact the submission is not accurate. Without doing that, the Defence has indicated that it had no objection to the submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Ms. Mahindaratne, it's not uncommon in this case and in this Tribunal that portions of a written statement are corrected and now, of course, the matter is whether the inaccuracy was of such a kind that it could not be repaired anymore, whether the attention of the Chamber should have been drawn to the fact that it might be difficult to get an attestation on the statement, the attestation, by the way, which contains three portions. The first one being whether it reflects what he said. Whether what he said at that time, whether he would give the same answers is, of course, another question. So, therefore, I'm not pronouncing any judgement on it but to say if there is no objection against admission of a 92 ter statement, although the other party knows that it might not be the final and the last version of the statement is -- whether that's inappropriate or not is still to be seen. You say it is; Mr. Misetic, I see already from his nodding that he disagrees with you, which doesn't come as a surprise. Anything else, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. That is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Briefly, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. First, I -- just as a matter of procedure, I still don't have an objection to the first 92 ter statement coming in as long as clarifications, corrections, et cetera, as we do routinely here, are made by the witness. There are also matters covered in the January OTP statement that aren't covered in the Defence statement, and for that reason, those matters should come in pursuant to Rule 92 ter. That's the first point. The second point, to respond substantively, is, I am virtually certain that when OTP calls witnesses who gave statements in 1995, that they don't go through the procedure of, first, not showing their witnesses their 1995 statement, questioning how much do they remember, how much is consistent with their own 1995 statement, for example. And then if the witness inaccurately answers questions that appear in his 1995 statement, I highly doubt that the OTP says, well, this is a statement we can't use because the witness doesn't recall telling us these matters, and there have been many witnesses who have come to -- with different answers to questions, have clarifications, et cetera. The fact of the matter is, the proper procedure is to put matters to the witness and let the witness tell us what the situation is. It shouldn't be left for counsel to make conclusions on behalf of the witness, and that is what we're talking about here. These are her conclusions -- Your Honour, let me just say, paragraph 12 of the statement she took today says, now referring to the two statements: "The meaning of what I told Mr. Ivankovic is same as the meaning of what I have told the OTP." At that point, what possible reason could there be for Ms. Mahindaratne not to take the statement out and say, well, do you think this portion of your OTP statement is consistent with what you said to the Defence; and if so, can you explain why. She's on notice that the witness apparently thinks that the two statements are similar. Now, again, this is about a search for the truth. Instead, we're in this one-way street now, if I can call it that way, where the witness has not been told that everyone has the second statement. He is going to be asked to make attestations under Rule 92 ter. The Defence will come up, show him the statement, and I would suggest to Your Honour there is a strong possibility that he's going to say, Yes, I gave that statement to the Court as well. The only issue -- I should say, it has only come up recently that Ms. Mahindaratne herself personally, with a witness as recently as two weeks ago, because the witness in cross-examination made a further correction based on the cross-examination that he didn't make at the beginning, she asked for a Rule 91 instruction against her own witness. In light of what she did with that witness, that's why I felt it was best for this witness that all these matters be fully disclosed, fully aired before we come to Court today or before he makes the attestation, so that we don't get a situation where now we're in cross-examination and now the witness is deemed to be a liar or asked to be given an instruction for perjury because Ms. Mahindaratne didn't put these matters to him before we came to Court. I fail to see the utility of this practice, and I again suggest that the proper course for this witness, before he makes a Rule 92 ter attestation, is to show him the Defence statement and then ask him whether he wishes to make any corrections or adopt what he said in the second statement as his further Rule 92 ter. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just add one thing here. Mr. Misetic made personal comment about the manner in which I proofed. The way we proof witnesses is we show -- give them the statements and they're asked to go through it carefully and to make any amendments or corrections, if there are any. And we do not discuss details the way -- in the manner that Mr. Misetic suggested. So if, for instance, a witness comes to Court and not having made a correction in his supplemental statement or in the course of proofing to his previous statement, that does not mean that I did not address those issues. It means that, having gone through the statement, the witness did not make that particular correction. We do not pinpoint and ask about every such detail. And Mr. Misetic is completely misrepresenting the manner in which we proof witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. While he said he was virtually certain, I refrain from asking him what was the basis for that, I just noticed that he says he was virtually certain, and that's how it is. Let's -- I feel the need that the Chamber briefly considers the matter. That might take one minute; that might also take ten minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I just -- having listened to the discussion, I did want to add one thing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a 92 ter statement, whether the Defence take it is or whether the Prosecution takes it, so the methodology should be the same. The witness should be given the statement. He should be able to look at it, make any corrections or changes that he or she needs to make to it and that's it. It should be the same whether a Prosecution statement or whether it is a Defence statement. In this case, since the Prosecution is tendering this witness and since the Prosecution was made known and publicly filed the 92 statement by the Defence, the same methodology should be apply and there should be really no difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand you well that you expect Ms. Mahindaratne to seek the attestations for the admission of the 92 ter statement filed by the Defence. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't, Your Honour. But I think it's -- a 92 ter statement is a 92 ter statement, whether it's from Defence or the Prosecution, and since it's a statement given by that particular witness outside of the courtroom in preparation for trial, I think the same methodology should apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As such, I do agree with you that a 92 ter statement, whether it comes from the Prosecution or from the Defence, is a 92 ter statement. That is written evidence rather than evidence given orally. Mr. Kay, you've been silent until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, I was silent, but it was a point very much in my mind that Mr. Kuzmanovic has made that when the witness is here he is a witness of the Court, and the statements, of course, may come from one party or the other party. In this sequence of events, the Defence here, because of nature of statement, they had disclosed it in advance to assist the Court bearing in mind what had happened recently. They could have kept the statement back and gone in cross-examination and matters taken a much longer course. The party presenting the witness now, the Prosecution, with that statement in hand, having been put on notice by the Defence that they were seeking for its admissibility under 92 ter, it seems to me quite clear, they should have put that statement to him so that he was in full possession of all the facts, and we didn't end up in the sort of circumstance that we find ourselves in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we are in the circumstances as we are at this moment, so we have to find a solution for that. And of course, the Chamber is also -- would also be concerned about attestation being given on statements which are contradicting. That is of course not a solution for the situation. I will briefly consider the matter with my colleagues. As I said it can take one minute, up to ten minutes -- yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just in light of your last comment, Your Honour. I'm not necessarily asking that he make attestations on our statement right now, although I would -- that would be my preference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But sooner or later, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if it is submitted as a 92 ter statement, then we have to seek attestations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I agree, but let me just make clear what my point is. My point is that right at the outset the Trial Chamber should get the best evidence possible. That's what I think we strive for in the courtroom, including the Bench. Even if is not a 92 ter Defence at the beginning, he should have been able to look at the statement and then say, oh, yes, either I agree with what I told the Defence; or, I need to make that correction in this paragraph in my statement. Then we would have the best evidence possible right at this beginning. I fear that, at the moment, just by going with the OTP statement, we're not getting the best evidence because it hasn't been put to the witness yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do see that, of course, another question arises whether under the present circumstances, in respect of some parts of the statements given, whether the application of Rule 92 ter is the appropriate Rule to be applied at this moment. I will consider the matter, the Bench will consider the matter, and we'll be back most likely before 3.00. The parties are requested to remain stand by. --- Break taken at 2.49 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said hopefully before 3.00. The Chamber has considered the procedural situation, in which we find ourselves at this moment, and has spent its time mainly on seeking a solution rather than trying to find out, who's right, who's wrong, who is to be blamed for what exactly. And the Chamber suggests that we proceed in the following way. If the parties would disagree, then we'll listen to any submissions, and if they give rise to reconsidering our suggestion, then we'll do so; if not, we'll stick to our suggestion. The way to proceed, in the view of the Chamber, is that we invite the Prosecution to call the witness, that I will then try, by putting some questions to the witness, to sort out the issue of when he, for the first time, saw the written version of his January statement, whether he saw it when he was interviewed in July. Just fact-finding on what happened with the statement, rather than to deal with any substance of it. If there's any need, the parties could, if they think that something essentially is missing, they could also, but within the strict limits, put some questions to the witness. We'll then know more or less what the situation is, as far as this witness is concerned, about rather important matters as to whether a statement was shown to him at a certain moment or whether just questions were put to him on the basis of a statement that was not shown to him at that time in July. We'll just hear from the witness what the situation was. After we have done that exercise, the Chamber invites the parties, in the strongest composition of their teams, to sit together, to identify also in view of the basis of the answers given by the witness which might add some information, to identify those portions in all three statements - that is the January statement, July statement, and October statement - to identify those portions where the parties consider the statements not to be consistent. Once these portions have been identified, to proceed by tendering the 92 ter statements with the exception of the inconsistent contradicting portions. And then, Ms. Mahindaratne, you will be invited to elicit oral testimony of the witness on any matter which, as a result of this identification of inconsistent portions, is taken out. So the contested issues there where there seems to be an inconsistency, where there seems to be a contradiction, is evidence that should be elicited orally, and then, of course, cross-examination will also be done in the usual way, and that we keep those portions of all three statements which are considered not to be inconsistent. That is the suggestion of the Chamber. Is there anything which should keep us off from proceeding this way?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just clarify two matters. One is, would the witness be allowed to see the July 2008 statement before he is questioned by you; and second is, would the Chamber be willing to tell him that he -- he had just as much right to meet with the Defence as he did with the Prosecution and that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no problem in telling the witness that speaking to both parties is not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And -- I should add that and there was no problem if the Defence showed him his OTP witness statement during its interview, that that is allowed by the rules and he shouldn't feel that there was something inappropriate about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, whether we would give him his July statement, if it is to identify that that's the statement he gave, fine; but of course we would not go to the substance because the questioning in the beginning is limited to what has happened; did you see your January statement at that time; was it given to you. Perhaps, I think we have an unsigned copy of it. At least -- I have an unsigned copy of the July statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Because original is in Croatian and is signed and you got an English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I take it that the signatures are there. But we'll -- for purposes of identifying the statement he gave, I see no problem. But as far as the substance, the content of the statement is concerned, I'd rather not do it, because there seems to be a difference of view between the witness and the parties on whether the statements are consistent yes or not, whether it is a similar statement or whether the statements are quite different. And rather than to ask him to analyse what is put on paper and whether that is really the same or something different, I rather have those portions be taken out of the statements and to elicit oral evidence from the witness on those portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't mean to show him or go through the substance of the disputed issues between the parties, just the paragraph in the Defence statement where he says, I am now being shown my OTP witness statement which does -- the portion that Ms. Mahindaratne read out and to ask him, did you tell this to the Defence in July of 1995 -- 2008, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, that is part -- I could tell him that we have a written statement which reads and then ... Any further comments on what is suggested as a solution? Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I go with such and -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we could proceed -- oh, yes, and the parties get half an hour to identify those portions. If they do not agree, then the Chamber will assist the parties in identifying inconsistent portions, not necessarily to be done in Court. That is a rather technical matter which could be dealt with out of Court because the Chamber is not going to accept a discussion up until Christmas on what is consistent and what is not consistent. The Chamber would like to proceed. Then, Ms. Mahindaratne, I take it that you call, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Mr. President, I take it once his name is recorded I would inform him that you would take over the -- the questions. I'm not to proceed with any questions until you have completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I even could ask him to state his full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Simic, I take it. Mr. Simic, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration will now be handed out to you by Mr. Usher. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Damir Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And your date of birth is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st of March, 1956.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. Usually, and perhaps that's what you expect, you would now be examined by Ms. Mahindaratne. But since we have a few questions in relations to the statements you've given, I will first put a few questions to you. Have you given a statement to investigators of the Office of the Prosecution on the 27th of January of this year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, when did you, for the first time, see the written version of the statement you have given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw it for the first time yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday. Did you not see it in July, when you were interviewed by Mr. -- I think it was Mr. Jovanovic [sic], when you were interviewed on behalf of the Defence? And let me add to this, there is nothing wrong if the Defence would show you a copy of the statement which they may have received by the Prosecution. They're fully entitled to do so. Did they show you your January statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we see in the statement that was taken and which has been given to the Chamber - let me first find it - and I read just a portion of -- of that statement as it was put on paper, you said: "I must emphasise," and that's what you told the -- what you told Mr. Ivanovic, as I understand. You told him: "I must emphasise that I gave a statement to the ICTY Office of the Prosecution on the 27th of January, 2008, which I haven't seen to this day. And on the basis of my notes which I had compiled during this interview, I sent a written amendment to my responses to the ICTY OTP." Is that what you told Mr. Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you then further were interviewed, was reference made to what you had stated in your January interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in your statement in July, we see that, on paper, reference is made to certain paragraphs or points in that January statement. Do you remember that portions of that statement, which everyone was fully entitled to show you, how do we have to understand your July statement in which it says in relation to point so-and-so, I say this and this and this, how could that have been done if no reference was made or if you had not been shown your January statement? That's a puzzle for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see the text itself. It was only referred to orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So when I asked you whether reference was made to that statement, it was done but orally, and you were not shown the statement itself, so you heard what was in the statement but you did not read what was in the statement. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we do understand that you have sent a letter to the Office of the Prosecution in which you further clarify your January statement. That letter, have you shown that to the -- Mr. Ivanovic, who was interviewing you, on behalf of the Defence? Was he aware of the letter that you sent and the content of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't show it to him, and I didn't mention it to him either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't believe it to be of importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now your supplementary witness statement which was taken this weak starts by saying: "I have been shown my statement that I gave on 27th of January," and you say, "this is the first time that I have seen the statement since I gave it to the representatives of the ICTY." Do I understand that, on that very day, which is the 8th of October, you, for the first time, have seen the statement on paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am looking at the parties, whether there are any additional questions in relation to what happened, as far as statements being shown, being given is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like me to show the statement, is that the matter you would like because you asked for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think it would be helpful just to have him -- is this the statement you signed in July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But then I would need the -- do we have the original in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We have the 1D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think I have to give it him. Mr. Registrar, it is 1D56-0005. I think we have to release it, Your Honour; it will take one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Simic, we have to overcome some technical difficulties but it will not take long. Mr. Simic, could you already look at the screen. Do you recognise the document in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is -- could you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the cover page of the statement I gave on the 24th of July, 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move to the last page. Do you recognise the signature at the bottom of that page? It has now disappeared but ... When I said the last page, I should have said the semi-last page. This is the page. Do you recognise the signature which appears in the middle of this page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it is whose signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did you put that signature -- where did you put it on this piece of paper? Where were you when you signed the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In what sense do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- I was informed that the interview took place in a restaurant, I think. Did you sign the statement in that restaurant, or did you sign that at another place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was at a notary public's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further questions? Mr. Simic, your examination goes a bit different from what is usually done. We'll now first take a break. The parties will have to consider certain matters. And after that break, which will take approximately half an hour, Ms. Mahindaratne will start your examination, and then later on, you'll be cross-examined by Defence counsel. I think it would be wise to take 35 minutes. Hard work for the parties to be done. If there's any problem for which the parties would like to have the assistance of the Chamber, we do not leave the building, we're here for the full 35 minutes. We will have a break until 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the Chamber was informed that the parties had reached agreement on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what portions would remain and what portions would be taken out of the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have put it in an e-mail and sent it to Mr. Nilsson. I have also provided a copy to Madam Registrar who will print it for you. But if you wish, I will also read it into the record as to what our agreement is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first have look at it. It depends on how much it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is short enough to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Prosecution and the Gotovina Defence agree that pursuant to Rule 92 ter, assuming all the attestations under the Rule are made, that the January 2008 statement given to the OTP, the July 2008 statement given to the Gotovina Defence, and the supplemental statement given to the OTP today, can be admitted into evidence with the following addendum, which is that the OTP will remove paragraph 17 from the January 2008 statement, will remove paragraph 16 from the October 9, 2008, supplemental statement, and that the OTP will lead live paragraph 5 of the supplemental statement given on October 9, 2008. The Gotovina Defence will lead live paragraph 2, page 2, of the July 2008 statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see that we -- because they're not numbered. Page 2, paragraph 2, is: "In the operative action Varivode and Gosici ..." Is that the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, no. This is now of the Defence statement, numbered page 2 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. I am --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We sent around last night and copied Mr. Nilsson on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have a witness statement, but no page numbers at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's what I mean. We sent one -- a corrected translation with page numbering at the bottom. You must have the older version. And there were also some translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's the paragraph you're talking --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's paragraph 2 of what is, in essence, the page after the cover page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is: "I have been presented ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We will lead that live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then if we go to two more pages in, which is the third page after the cover page. The Gotovina will lead live paragraph 2, which begins: "After I was presented ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The Gotovina Defence will remove the next paragraph, which begins: "Regarding the order ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And will remove the paragraph after that, which begins: "With respect to the claims ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then, finally, Your Honour, the parties have agreed that OTP will not address matters in its direct examination that the Gotovina Defence will lead live in its cross-examination, which specifically means paragraph 2, page 2, of the July 2008 statement and paragraph 2, page 4, of the July 2008 statement. However, OTP is free to address these matters in redirect examination, with the permission of the Court obviously, should the Gotovina Defence lead them live in cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, one question, if you lead this evidence live in cross, if Ms. Mahindaratne would address these matters in redirect, would that be considered a kind of a cross-examination or would it be examination-in-chief? I'm just asking, what your view on that is. It sounds to me as if, for that particular portion, Ms. Mahindaratne would be in a position more or less to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that actually paragraph 2, page 2, is a new matter because it relates to whether he had seen his statement before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, page 4, I believe addresses matters that are in his January statement and for that reason -- or at least related to his January statement so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll come to that at a later stage. If you could reach agreement on what your position exactly is at that moment, that would be appreciated. If not, the Chamber of course will guide you. Then I think we could start, Ms. Mahindaratne. There was one question, by the way, I've forgotten to ask the witness. That is, whether any documents were shown to him, although his January statement was not shown to him in July, because we find in the supplementary statement, supplemental statement, that no documents were shown to him, whereas very explicit in the July statement is where he says, This document which was shown to me by the OTP and which is shown to me today again, where it is very explicit. I had not asked him. If that's a matter that would bother you, I take it that you will take care of that. Although it is a portion which is taken out, I think. Yes, that's the two paragraphs taken out regarding the order I mentioned in point 17 and which I saw again today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's being taken out. The preceding paragraph also references a document that he was presented, and as I lead it live, I would be happy to address that with him as foundation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although there he is not that explicit that it's being shown to him again today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, we've removed it because the related paragraph in the OTP statement is also being removed, so it's a non-issue at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just, on that point, draw your attention to paragraph 11 of the supplemental statement. The witness's position at proofing was that he was not shown any documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That -- then, Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- examine the witness. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What are we going to do about the admission of 92 ter statements because there were no objections. There are still no objections. We know that some portions have been taken out. Would it not be the best to first examine the witness and then to say, apart from what you've told us today, is -- for the remainder are your statements, do they reflect -- he hasn't read them all?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is what, Mr. President, I wanted to point out, that as far as the OTP January statement and the supplemental statement are concerned, he has read them again. But I don't know if he has had the opportunity to read the Defence statement recently, and correct, if he wishes to make any corrections or amendments to the Defence statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- again, I've leave it in your hands, but we now have agreement. I certainly would like him to read through his July 2008 statement. As far as I know, he hasn't seen it since July 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But give it to him in the next break, wouldn't that be a good idea --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay, yes. And, Your Honour, if I may say somewhat sheepishly, I did not catch the issue in paragraph 11 of the supplemental as it relates to my leading paragraph 2, page 4, of July 2008. So if I could discuss that one paragraph with my colleagues during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, paragraph 11 was the reason why I raised the issue in relation to that taken out paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's focus -- Mr. Simic, the break was -- Mr. Simic, the break was a little bit longer than expected; apologies for that. You will be now further examined by Ms. Mahindaratne. Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I ask if I could lead him on paragraph 11 of the supplementary statement in the course of my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask then that if we could hold off on that until he gets the statement during the break so he can go through it before -- and then after he has read through the statement, she ask lead him on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think that that is a requirement. I would be just asking him a question, straightforward question he'd be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said that it was a question which I had a mind to put to him. Let me then start for one second and seek verification of what we find in paragraph 11 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can I ask that he be pointed to that, whatever it is, in the July statement and asked to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will put the two to him and then I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, again, I have one or two questions for you. In your supplementary statement which was taken this week, you said the following, and you were talking about the interview that you had with the Defence in July. And you said -- you told that when the statement was complete that it was certified by a notary public in Biograd. And then you said: "I did not bring any notes with me and Mr. Ivankovic did not show me any documents during the interview." Now, in the written report of the interview, I just read one line for you, and it is about an order -- an order of the 9th of August, 1995. You said the following: "Regarding the order I mentioned in point 17," that is this 9th of August order, "and which was presented to me by the ICTY investigators and which I saw again today ..." and then you give an answer. This part of your July statement suggests that you were shown that order not only in January but also in July, whereas in your supplementary statement you say, "No documents were shown to me." Could you help us out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I had seen that specific order before without anyone having shown it to me, presenting it to me. Maybe it had been accessible to me. I don't know how to explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand your answer to be that when you said "which I saw again today," that that does not necessarily mean that it was shown to you during the interview, but that you might have looked at it on that day but not during the interview. Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say it is your answer that that possibly may have happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we have dealt with the matter, Ms. Mahindaratne, Mr. Misetic. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I, with your permission. I don't know if the witness's response -- whether he understood what he was being exactly asked, that when it says -- you say it is your answer that it is possible may have happened. I don't know what his -- what his understanding was. May I ask a question or may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that -- let me ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you may move to your next subject, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, now you already testified that you provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 27th January 2008. On that occasion, and I'm referring to the interview with the Office of the Prosecutor in January, did you examine three documents and provide explanations regarding those documents?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me specifically what documents you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the note you had compiled on 25th October regarding your investigations, and the statement you made to the ministry of -- I'm sorry, Ministry of Interior -- the statement you made regarding that investigation into the Gosici incident in 2001, the statement you made in 2001, and another military document. Do you recall examining those documents and providing explanations in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, if you could show me those documents, then I would be able to tell you. I would like to see what it is --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. --

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: -- about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will take you there. Let me just first go through some other questions. Now, last evening, did you examine the statement you made to the Office of the Prosecutor in January 2008?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Having examined that statement, did you provide further clarifications and amendments by way of a supplementary statement? I'm referring to last evening.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I saw that statement and I gave an additional statement which was addressed to Mr. Foster, but you did not get it. That was my objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Simic, you misunderstood me. Last evening, when you went through your statement given in January, did you also provide an additional statement last evening which was recorded? I'm not referring to the letter you sent; I'll get to that. But I'm talking about last evening, having examined your statement of January 2008, did you provide a further statement?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, was that statement recorded in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: You mean the January 2008 statement? Is that the statement you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, no. The statement that you made in -- made last evening, was it recorded in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, after the proofing session finished for the day, did you read that statement, the one that was recorded in Croatian last evening?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I did. I did read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, having read that, did you find that it accurately reflected what you had stated in the course of the proofing meeting last evening?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did find that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, is it possible for you to perhaps pull up your chair so that could you speak closer to the microphones. And then did you sign the supplementary statement as being true and accurate last evening?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This morning, did you examine that supplementary statement again and confirm that it was true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar [sic], may I have document 5487, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Simic, subject to the clarifications that you provided, clarifications and amendments you provided to your January 2008 statement, subject to those, are the contents of your January 2008 statement true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: This statement of 27 January 2008 is a statement to which I sent my objections to Mr. Brian, and there have been some corrections and amendments made. I think that it would be complete and accurate if those corrections and amendments are included.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: They would be included, Mr. Simic. Now, last evening you provided clarifications and amendments to the statement, did you not? Last evening.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And I will also -- soon after this I will also tender your letter into evidence but subject to -- my question to you is: Subject to the clarifications and amendments in your supplementary statement and your letter sent to Mr. Foster, is your statement of 27 January 2008 true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if you were asked those questions that were asked of you by the members of the Office of the Prosecutor in January and last evening again today in court, would your responses be the same?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that they would.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that your statement of 27 January 2008?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is its cover page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And is that your signature at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And Mr. Registrar, if you could go to the not the last page but the one before the last page, please. I'm sorry, it should be Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, is that your signature at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now are you taking all three at one time? Are we talking about the January statement plus the letter plus the supplementary statement, or -- because you said --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I was going to, then, call up the supplementary statement, then the document, then the letter, and then tender them into evidence, but if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you -- perhaps if the witness has looked at everything --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and then we can do it under three numbers. Then we have a complete picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar [sic], may I call document 5500, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you will see in a moment a document on your screen. Do you recognise -- recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that your signature at the bottom of the cover page?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If could you move to the next page, please. I think that is the last -- the one before the last page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is this your statement given last evening?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do you recognise your signature at the bottom of the document on this last page?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, are the contents of this statement given last evening true to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if those questions that were asked you of last evening were asked again in court today, would your responses be the same?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: They would. They would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, may I call document 5501, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Simic, you mentioned yesterday, and it is recorded in paragraph 13 of your supplementary statement, that you sent a letter to the Office of the Prosecutor providing a list of amendments to your statement. Did you hand over that document to the Office of the Prosecutor this morning?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I handed it over to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And last evening you mentioned that -- that this document was sent to the OTP under registered cover, and you said that you may have had the postal receipt, which is also recorded in the supplementary statement. Now, were you able to find that receipt, to be -- to be given to the Office of the Prosecutor this morning?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't because the receipt is in Croatia. I don't have it -- I don't have it with me here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is it in your possession in Croatia or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, isn't the issue whether this is the letter he wrote?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I was just about to ask it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but whether he has receipt or not, if this the is letter he wrote then we --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I just wanted to demonstrate the fact that we have -- we have searched and we have not found this document in our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, but if this is the letter he referred to earlier which he said was an important amendment or clarification to his letter, then that's the core issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I only brought it out because Mr. Misetic, in fact, inquired from me during the break. That is the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. Perhaps I should not have intervened. But let go to the -- what appears to be the core of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can just say that I just inquired. There is it no dispute --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- so there's no need. I accept their representation that they didn't receive it until yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, is this the document that you sent to the OTP in March 2008?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could go to the last page, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that your signature at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And are the contents of this document true to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you write this letter on your own?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I said so this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe perhaps this is a moment to submit the statement of 2007 [sic] with supplemental statement of 8 October together with this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no 2007 statement, but I take it that you're referring to the January 2008 statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I refer to the January 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I take that we'll decide on admission of the three together and that, if taken together, is there any -- is there any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Nevertheless, as they are now on our screen, Ms. Mahindaratne, they cannot be admitted because have you to redact them in accordance with your agreement which means that paragraph 16 and 17 -- no, no, paragraph 17 of the January statement should be taken out; paragraph 16 of the supplemental statement should be redacted; and I take it that paragraph 5 of the supplemental statement stays but we'll further elaborate it in your examination-in-chief. So, therefore, no -- we could decide on admission once you have uploaded the redacted versions of the statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will do that at close of sessions tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's already provisionally provide numbers for them. Madam Registrar, the January 2008 statement, still to be redacted would be number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number P967, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the supplemental statement dated the 8th of October, 2008, would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number P968, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we have the letter, the letter which is the 12th of March, 2008, sent to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number P969, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P969 is admitted into evidence. And the other two documents will be admitted into evidence once a redacted version has been uploaded. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution also included three documents in the 92 ter submission of which I move to withdraw one document because it has already been tendered into evidence by the Defence, and that would be document number 3216, 65 ter, which has already been tendered into evidence as D281.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the remaining ones would be 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: 65 ter 5488. Mr. President, since the witness wanted to have a look at the document, I will quickly show these two documents -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, may have I document number 5488, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I just asked you a little while ago whether you recall reviewing some documents when you were interviewed by the OTP in January and in providing explanations regarding those documents in your statement and you wanted to take a look at those documents. Do you remember examining this document in January -- on 27 January and providing an explanation regarding this document in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are no objections, Madam Registrar, 65 ter 5488 would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit number P970, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P970 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if I could have document number 5489, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you recall examining this particular document on 27th January 2008 and providing an explanation regarding this document in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Can you show me another page of this document as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could move to page 2 and if you could just skip through it; it's only five pages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is -- do you recall examining this document on 27th January 2008 and providing an explanation in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we proceed on that, you said it's only five pages. And -- oh, the English is five pages. I see the original is three pages. Yes, that is clear to me now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 65 ter 5489.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit number P971, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P971 is admitted into evidence. Now, Ms. Mahindaratne, the purpose of showing these documents to the witness is also to give substance to his statements. Now, the other document, you said we don't have to deal with, because it is already in evidence. Of course, if we could link that to the statement of the witness, then at least we would know that this was the document he gave a statement about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well Mr. President. Madam Registrar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although it needs not to be admitted anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if I could have document number D281, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you recall examining this document? And I will ask Madam Registrar to go on to the next page so that you can take a look at it. Do you recall examining this document on 27 January 2008 and referring to the document?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I reviewed the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's already in evidence, Mr. President. I will ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, may I have the witness's statement, P967, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I'd like to show your statement given to us, to the OTP, in 2008, January.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could move to next page, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just -- I'm sorry to interrupt. Just to clarify for the record, and in case I'm mistaken about something, but the document that was previously shown to the witness is part of the paragraph 17 that has been removed from the statement. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I'd like to you look at paragraph 3 of your statement, where you have provided information regarding the structure of the 72nd Military Police Battalion. My question to you is: Did each of the military police companies, and you refer to general military police companies there, did each of the military police companies have crime police sections attached to the companies?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: All independent companies, that's to say, the ones that were outside battalions, had crime police sections as part of them, according to their establishments.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, my question is -- I'm not referring to the independent companies but I'm referring to the companies, the general military police companies within the 72nd Military Police Battalion. Did those companies have military crime police sections attached to them? I'm not saying -- when you say "company," I'm not referring to huge companies, maybe a section, two or three officers or ...

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: We are probably at odds. We probably misunderstand each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My objection is to lack of specificity. I think there has been testimony already on this issue, and if we could -- I think it will clear it up if we talk specifically by companies that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well. I will ask about two particular companies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now your -- the company that your -- you belonged to was the 4th Company, Sibenik, which was within the 72nd Military Police Battalion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: That was the 4th Company within the 72nd Military Battalion. There was no corps there. It was attached to the battalion, and its title was the 4th Company.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did the 4th Company have its own crime police?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: The 4th Sibenik Company had a crime police department, as per establishment, which comprised both commissioned and non-commissioned officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And who was the head of that department, of the 4th Company, Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you inquiring to the crime police section or to the company?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The crime police section, Mr. President. I used the word department for that reason because the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would be very specific in your question, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ask you, Mr. Simic, who was in command of the crime police section of the 4th Company you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me be even more precise. With the 4th Company there was a military police service. I was at the head of that -- rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, crime police section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And whom did you report to?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: As the head of that crime police section, I was directly subordinated to Boris Milas, according to the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Who was Captain Mrkota?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Captain Nenad Mrkota was the commander of the 4th Sibenik Company.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you receive orders from him?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you report to him?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Only as far as the work of the service was concerned. I reported to him on the work of the service.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you say -- can you be a little bit more specific, Mr. Simic. When you say "I reported to him on the work of the service," what are you referring to? Is it the tasks of the crime police or what exactly are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
