utterances.text: Those were the daily assignments of the crime police. I reported on the problems detected, activities carried out and activities planned. Now, as for the monthly reports of the crime police, I sent that directly to the battalion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness. If he could repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, could you repeat the last part of your answer because the interpreter didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I passed over to Captain Mrkota all the daily planned activities for a particular day. This was at the morning briefings within the company. As for the monthly reports on the work and efficiency and the activities carried out by the crime police service, I reported to Boris Milas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, is it possible for you to speak up a little or get closer to the microphones so that, you know, the interpreters could hear you properly. Thank you. And who was Boris Milas?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of the section of the crime police in the 72nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. That was going to be my question. Now, what was the area of responsibility of the 4th Company, Sibenik, after the liberation of the territory on 4th and 5th August? I'm not talking about the area of responsibility in peacetime but this is after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the question. I don't know -- the last sentence, I'm not sure what that distinction is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but much depends on when you consider the Operation Storm to be finished, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your earlier question was, however, clear and that you said after the 4th or 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'll stay with that, Mr. President. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I'm sorry if I confused you. My question was: After the territory was liberated on 4th and 5th August, 1995, what was the area of responsibility of the 4th Company, Sibenik, the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: The military police of the 4th Company, Sibenik, had the area from Sibenik to Loznica and, in the hinterland, all the way to Drnis before the action. After the action, pursuant to various orders, the AOR changed. As I had a lot to do within my service, resolving various problems, I was unable to keep track of that. This was not part of my duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm not criticising for you -- for that at all, Mr. Simic. It was just a question which the Trial Chamber would be interested in knowing. If could you say -- can you at least by way of municipalities, let me ask you, did the -- did the area of Drnis come within the area of responsibility of the 4th Company, Sibenik, after the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I know that because I sent an officer and a non-commissioned officer out into the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did the area of Kistanje come within the area of responsibility of the 4th Company, Sibenik, after 5th August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know about that. I did not send my men over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm not asking about whether you sent your men, but do you know if the 4th Company, Sibenik, military police of the -- I'm referring to the 4th Company, Sibenik, your company, whether they had any personnel deployed in Kistanje. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I can't claim that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, within the 4th Company, Sibenik, were you the most senior officer of the crime police?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, may I have document P880, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you recall examining this document yesterday and this morning?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if you could go to -- in the English version, page 25. And in the B/C/S, 7728.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: While that is being brought up, Mr. Simic, are you familiar with the provisions relating to the work of the military crime police, which are included in this document? I'm not going to ask you without referring you to the particular Articles, but are you generally familiar?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are these the rules that governed your activity during 1995? When I say "your activity," I'm referring to the work of the military crime police.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'd like to you look at Article 61, Mr. Simic, where it refers -- I'll just read it out. You can read your version. "An authorised official of the military police may arrest a person if there is reason to believe that the crime committed falls within the jurisdiction of a Military Court when there are grounds for this provided for by the law that prescribes a criminal investigation." The next paragraph reads: "The arrested person must be brought before the investigating judge in charge without delay with a report on the crime committed and the grounds for the person's arrest." And in the English version, if we could go to next page, Madam Registrar. The final paragraph of that Article reads: "The authorised official of the military police must inform the senior officer of the arrested member of the Croatian army of the arrest within 24 hours ..." and then there is further text. My question actually is about that. Now, how was the information transmitted by the military police to the senior officer of the arrested member? And I presume that senior officer is the senior officer of the unit to which the arrested member belonged. How was that information conveyed by the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: An authorised official of the military police, where a person was arrested for a criminal offence, regardless of the offence, it could be murder or anything else, reported to his own duty service of the offence committed, and the duty service of the company that arrested person belonged to reported that information to the superior of the person arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question was: How was that information conveyed? Was there a formal mechanism, in writing, or just an ad hoc manner, by telephone? How was that information conveyed?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Information may have been, could have been transmitted by telephone but it had to be necessarily followed by a written report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what was the superior officer of the arrested person supposed to do with that information when he received that report, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. That was not part of my job.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Let move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if I could -- Mr. President, may I have this document tendered into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Now we have -- first of all, isn't it already into evidence; that is my first question. The second question is: If you quote one line or three lines or five lines of an Article, should we then receive 70 pages or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it is in evidence. I made a mistake, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Madam Registrar, may I call document 5493, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you recall examining this document last evening and this morning?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you were asked specifically to take a look at chapters 1, 12, 13, 15, and 17?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, what is available on -- in the English language is just those chapters. It is a huge document and I wish to draw the attention of the Chamber to those particular chapters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please add, then, the cover page of that document, because now it's a document without any -- let me check.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I was under the impression that was there, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me just have a look. I see one original, and I see three translations uploaded, apparently, of certain portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 65 ter 2252 and 2253 may assist others with other numbering.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will have the cover page uploaded, Mr. President. The text of the chapters I referred to are included in the translations. What is not available is the cover page, and I will have that uploaded at the close of business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you also check the 65 ter numbers to -- Mr. Kay just mentioned to which the Chamber has no access.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. That's a mistake that those -- the 65 ter numbers Mr. Kay referred to are the old 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there are -- Ms. Mahindaratne, I read, and I'm just -- I'm just reading what you presented, is -- yes. Yes. That they were previously registered under other numbers; I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I just ask the question on this, Mr. President? I just want it bring your note -- draw your attention to the fact that the translation doesn't entirely cover the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. And we will receive a translation of the cover page to be attached to one of the three portions of the English translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Simic, having examined those particular chapters, can you say were those rules -- and that is in chapter -- the provisions in chapter 1, chapter 12, 13, 15, and 17, did those rules apply during 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but I think the witness should be shown why that question is being put to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'll ask that because the witness is aware of that -- I pointed it out during proofing. I will ask that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But of course what you said to him during proofing is not something --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, I'm sorry, Mr. President. I should ask one more question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to which the Chamber is privy. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Simic, this is a document published in December 1995. My question to you is: Having examined those chapters, did you find that if the rules which were contained in this document, published in December 1995, were they also applicable or did they govern your activity during 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, for the sake of clarity. Since December 1995 is in 1995, I think it should be clear what period of time we're talking about, and what rules specifically as compared to what other rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I referred to the rules, Mr. President, but if Mr. Misetic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic, I see that apparently you have -- you have a sharp eye on possible complications which can be resolved in cross-examination, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, you heard what Mr. Misetic said, Ms. Mahindaratne -- you could even avoid.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President, I will ask him specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in your activity work of the crime police during the period 4th August to end of September 1995, did these rules also apply, in the sense that the rules that were governed by -- the rules that governed your work during that period, were they one and the same, as contained in these provisions, in those particular chapters that I referred to you?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Whether they were observed, that is not at all a question. It was my obligation to observe those rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, my question was if, in fact, these rules were the same that were applicable during the period 4th August to end of September, 1995. My question is, although it is published in December 1995, did -- were the rules similar to what you followed during 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I'll try to answer this way. I was a policeman in August, on the 4th of August, and at the end of September as well. So I had to abide by all those rules in -- at all those times.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And those rules that you abided by, are these the rules?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if -- may I be permitted to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just a question that I honestly don't know the answer to. Is there a codification published prior to December 1995 or is this -- is the Prosecution saying this is the first codification?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are not aware of it. We have asked the Croatian government for the handbook for the period applicable to -- relevant to the indictment, but this is what we have got. So if, in fact, we did have codification before that, I would be tendering that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is no, Mr. Misetic. At least the Prosecution is not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then I guess it goes to weight but not admissibility but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, questions have been put to the witness, he has reviewed the document, he answered the questions, so therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Mahindaratne, before we continue, you -- I'm just trying to, you said -- you asked the witness whether he had reviewed chapters 1, 12, 13, 15, and 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if I look at three portions of translations, I find chapter 1, at least; I find 12; I find 15; and I think, 16. 13 and 17, could you tell me in what portion of the document this -- what portion of the translation this is found. And I have the numbers of the translations. One is 03621498. That, as far as I can see, is chapter 1. I have same first four digits and then 1522, which looks as if it were 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not find 13 there. Then we have same first four digits and then 1527, which is 15, followed by 16 and no 17. How do you expect the Chamber to evaluate the testimony of the witness where different chapters, at least not all of them the same chapters, are given to us, compared to what the witness testified about?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I was under the impression that the translations of those two chapters were there. But therefore, I see the problem. Could the document be marked for identification and I will see that the translations of those two sections are uploaded before cross-examination starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The handbook of procedures for the criminal military police, 1996 -- let me just check. And you said it was ... Madam Registrar that would receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit number P972, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is marked for identification and keeps that status for the time being. Ms. Mahindaratne, if I'm able to check all this in -- in one or two minutes, wouldn't it be a good idea that you check your material also before you examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I have, Madam Registrar, document number 4671, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, meanwhile I'm looking at the original of the last documents, which bears the year 1996, which apparently was sent or at least we find some kind of a letter --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- apparently from the Ministry of Defence at an earlier date in 1995. If you would upload that as well so that could give us valuable information about applicability or whether it follows any or document --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so I'm not seeking the whole of the document but page 03621495, if you would review whether that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In fact, those were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- contains any valuable information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In fact, those were the pages that I'd requested a translation, Mr. President. It was in fact the first four pages of the document so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you could add them to the document which is now marked for identification in translation as well. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, but just so that you're fully aware of what the issues between the parties might be, we will -- I have looked at and we will take the position that there was another code that applied here during the relevant time-period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you -- did you have the opportunity to examine this document last evening and this morning?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I did. What was offered to me, I did review.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And is this the duty log-book of the 4th Company, Sibenik, of the 72nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yeah, this is the cover of that book.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And we will go through the next few pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, what is available in this document is only for the period 4th August to 11th August. That's for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, having examined this document last night, did you find that the contents accurately reflected the tasks of the 4th Company, Sibenik, for the period 4th to 11th August?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask for foundation on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness is a senior officer of the 4th Company, Sibenik, and he is, in fact, in the supplementary statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- could you refer us to a paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. It's not -- I will ask a question before I ask that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you explain how this duty log-book was maintained, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Each one of these eight officers and -- and non-commissioned officers who were registered here conducted a duty for an uninterrupted 24 hours. They also had assistants would who take over during rest periods. All the events over the period of 24 hours would be jotted down, entered in written form in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And were you at any stage also involved in maintaining the log-book?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I absolutely used that book, and I entered all the events for the day that took place in the company in the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is there any mechanism or is there a duty upon the person who maintains the book at the time to ensure that the entries entered here are accurate?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. That is why only officers are on duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And having examined this document last night, did you have any reason to doubt the accuracy of the entries in this document?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I believe that whoever made the entries into the book did so accurately.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I enter this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P973, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P973 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And while we're on this document, Madam Registrar, could you move to the English translation page, page number 7. And B/C/S would be 1175.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, at -- in the English translation, the date starts from the previous page. That is 6th August 1995. Mr. Simic, the entry for 2050 on 6th August indicates that nine military policemen were sent to Kistanje. Are you able to offer some information as to whether this is a patrol being sent or is it a platoon being sent to be permanently relocated to Kistanje or was this a check-point being set up?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was on duty that day. It can be seen on the next page, probably. If it is not a problem, I would like to see the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no doubt for me -- there is no reason for me it doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. My question was whether you would be able to say by looking at the entry that the nine persons who are being -- nine military policemen who are being sent to Kistanje on 6th August what was it -- is it being sent -- are they being sent as a military police patrol or a platoon being relocated to or deployed to Kistanje or is it a -- are they being sent to set up a check-point in Kistanje? Would you be able to offer some information? What kind of deployment was that; that's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I saw it yesterday for the first time and now I'm looking at it for the second time. My presence is not indicated in these documents anywhere, so I have no way of knowing unless I was there at the time. There is no way I -- I could know. I would have to have been there and I wasn't there. It was not my stint of duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was outside working hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Simic, if you would just tell us that you don't know, whether you could have known, if that's a matter Ms. Mahindaratne wants to further explore, she'll certainly do so. She asked you what kind of deployment it was and you don't know. Just tell us that and then wait for the next question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: While we're on that page, Mr. Simic, could you look at the entry for 1425. And it refers to a fax from 72nd Military Police Battalion came and there is another reference there. I only ask because through this log-book there are numerous entries of faxes coming from the 72nd Military Police Battalion. Now, would you be able to say as to what kind of communication - and I'm not asking of the substance - what type of communications came from the 72nd Battalion to the 4th Company, Sibenik, by way of faxes? Was it order or -- I'm trying to get you to describe, if possible, what they were.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: At 1425, a fax arrived from the military police of the 72nd Battalion. Information about the cancellation of wanted posters because they were issued at a level of all companies. The companies where those people operated and moved.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let me just ask you this way. How did orders from the 72nd Battalion arrive at the 4th Company, Sibenik? What was the means through which orders were conveyed to your Company?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Not to me but to the commander of the company. That depended on the confidentiality level, whether it could be send by fax or some other way. Orders certainly did not come by fax. It was either by other communication mean, by Rebus or code.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You say -- your response wasn't that clear. You said that depending on the confidentiality level, whether it could be sent by fax or some other way. Orders certainly did not come by fax. My question is: Were orders conveyed by fax? And I'm not sure what you exactly said because you said depending on the confidentiality, it could be sent by fax or some other way. And the next phrase was: "Orders certainly did not come by fax." I'm asking to you say which did you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All orders which operationally had to do with the Sibenik Company did not come by fax. They would either come -- be brought by messenger by courier or by Rebus because they bore a specific secrecy degree because they were confidential.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What about the daily taskings?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Daily tasks were something else. For instance, this one, the cancellation of a wanted circular. An order regarding the sending of a convoy, that is not a true order in the military sense; it is more of an instruction. Like also in the case of the regulation of some part of traffic or something like that, that would be conveyed by fax.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, can we go to page number 10, please, in the English version, and B/C/S 1177.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, if you could look at the entry for -- this is for -- in the English version it starts -- the date is noted on the -- the previous page, right at the bottom, 10 August 1995. If you note the entry at 1720 it says: "Mail arrived," and there is a reference number given. It says, "Subject: Order to comply with military disciplinary measures from the commander of ZP, Military District Split." Now, can you explain that this is an order that has arrived at the 4th Company, Sibenik, directly from the Military District command or has it been sent here to your company via the normal chain of command through the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object on multiple grounds. It mischaracterizes the order itself, which is in evidence. Furthermore, foundation as to whether this witness knows, how he knows, it is -- she's presented it as an order to the company which, it's in evidence, and there should be some foundation for that claim.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the entry itself speaks for it, the document is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness. Would you, please, Ms. Mahindaratne. Please put just to the witness what we read here and then ask questions about the matter, and, of course, the question should always be to the extent the witness knows. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, are you able to look at this entry and tell us, as to if this order has been sent directly or if it has arrived via a chain of command through the battalion, to the 72nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: As we can see from the entry, at 1720, mail with that number arrived there. It doesn't say how it arrived though. It could have been brought directly to the company by a courier, or a courier from the encryption service could have brought it over. I don't know what this is about, whether this was an escort that was to be provided for transport, whether it was securing of a military area or providing security to a person. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recall around this time, did you -- was this order discussed with you by your commander, Mrkota?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the witness aware of the order? He just told us that he doesn't know what it is about, and then he mentioned a few possibilities which are difficult to reconcile with the description of the order as we read it in the entry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will rephrase, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, at any stage did your company commander, Mrkota, discuss an order referring to military disciplinary measures received from the Military District Command Split with you?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. As far as I know, he didn't. There was no need for him -- no reason for him to discuss this with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could move to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness explain his last answer. You said there was no need to discuss it with you. Why was there no need to discuss it with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a senior lieutenant of the HV by rank and I was the head of the military police crime service. I was not a commander of a platoon or anything that would have boiled down to the operational level. I did not have my own troops, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if could I ask a follow-up question on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In response to question from the Bench, you said: "I did not have my own troops, so to speak." Why did you use that term, did you understand this order on military disciplinary measures to refer to the conduct of troops?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No, no. I spoke in the context of your question concerning Mrkota, company commander. I could not act in operational terms because I did not have my own army. I could not proceed to carry out assignments. I could not go and erect or tour check-points or go patrolling, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So who -- which sections in the 4th Company, Sibenik, would Captain Mrkota direct this order to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first try to identify whether the witness knows what this order is. Because, otherwise, it is all a bit in the air.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I should ask one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or if you would say, in general, are aware of orders issued to comply with military disciplinary measures, and do you know how these orders were passed to others. Then that's a question dependant on the answer to the first question. You could put the second question. But you're talking about this order --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sorry Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... not yet established that the witness knows what this order is about, apart from what he reads in the description in this log.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I will just ask him a question based on his response.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you said: "I could not go and erect or tour check-points or go patrolling, that sort of thing." Now, if such activity was required, that is, setting up check-points or go patrolling, what sections of the 4th Company, Sibenik, would Captain Mrkota have to address? Such orders in general, and I'm not referring to this order.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Captain Mrkota could convey orders down to the lower levels, which was platoon commanders who could, in their own right, convey orders to squad commanders. That's the way the chain went.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And how many platoons did the 4th Company, Sibenik, have during the period 4th to 5th August, to end September 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Three platoons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Approximately how many personnel were attached to each of these platoons?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Roughly 30 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you say "roughly 30 men," roughly 30 men per platoon? Could you be specific?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Every platoon had around 30 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President this would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A suitable time to have break. Then we will have a break and we'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, as the senior-most officer of the crime police of the 4th Company, Sibenik, did your subordinate personnel within the crime police report to you on their daily activity?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question? Or clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, your testimony was that you were the senior-most officer of the crime police section of the 4th Company, Sibenik. That's correct, isn't it? Now, my question is, did your subordinate officers and personnel within the crime police section of the 4th Company, Sibenik, report to you on their daily activities, or their daily taskings? I'm talking about the crime -- military police crime -- military police taskings.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Having had the highest rank, I was at the head of the service and they were duty-bound to report to me. And in our daily morning briefings, we would have discussed the tasks and the activities of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to look at, Mr. Simic --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could move to page 11 of the English version of the document on the screen. And the B/C/S version is -- actually, we can stay on the same page in the B/C/S version. Same page, Madam Registrar, if we could move to the right-hand corner of the page. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you note the entry at 2255, where it is recorded that: "Duty officer of the 72nd Military Police Battalion Pavlovic informed that some houses were set on fire by HV members in the villages Kricke Donje and Kricke Gornje." And then it reads: "The R-platoon in Drnis was notified via MUP colleagues." Now, do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If there was an investigation into -- some form of investigation into this particular incident, were you -- would you as the head of the crime military police of the 4th Company, Sibenik, be informed of that investigation?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I would. If my men in Drnis were in charge of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And were there any crime military police who were outside your command present in Drnis?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I believe there were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Drnis, you said -- your testimony was that Drnis was within the area of responsibility of the Sibenik -- the 4th Company, Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I said that I -- our AOR went as far as Drnis. After Operation Storm, certain platoons were detached. I didn't know about Kistanje. And I deployed certain non-commissioned officers of the military police crime -- of the military crime police to be in charge there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, my question is, Mr. Simic, this is an entry for 10th August 1995. That is, after the liberation of the territory.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How many -- how many officers or personnel attached to your crime police department were sent by you to Drnis?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: You mean from Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: From -- from your crime police section of the 4th Company, Sibenik, how many officers did you send to be attached to the platoon in Drnis?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: When the Drnis platoon went, they accompanied them, or perhaps they went or followed them a day or two later.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question is: How many officers did you send?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: One commissioned officer and one non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What was their responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: They were supposed to be in charge of the Drnis AOR, of the AOR of that platoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Drnis - this is after the liberation - Drnis came within the AOR of the 4th Company, Sibenik, military police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, I will try to explain this. The 4th Company detached one platoon out into Drnis. Two men of the military crime police followed them, and they had their own responsibilities. This was not the AOR of the 4th Company but the AOR of that platoon which was there temporarily. So this was not our structure or unit. It was merely sent out detached into the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, those two -- you said the responsibility of those two officers that you sent were the activities -- the area of responsibility was Drnis. Now, if any criminal investigations were to be conducted in Drnis, would that duty fall upon those two officers?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And were there any other police, military police, crime military police, attached to that platoon in Drnis? Except for -- other than those two officers.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did those two officers report to you?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, there -- I'm not certain anymore whether they reported to the commander of the platoon there or to me. But I believe that they went through their platoon and reported that way through the platoon to the battalion. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: As head of the criminal police section of the company, who -- in order -- who would receive information about the daily taskings of the crime police, crime military police or all the platoons and all the sections within the Sibenik 4th Company?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you repeat your answer, Mr. Simic. The interpreter didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: All the companies, all the independent platoons, including the Drnis independent company which had its AOR, its duty services, its commander, and two duty service officers, they acted independently, and most probably they reported on their daily work to the battalion, which was stationed in Split. And the battalion, in turn, reported to the military police administration in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you in any way informed of what those officers were reporting to the platoon leader?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No. Had I been reported to, I would have included the results their work into my reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So where would the -- the work of those two officers be reported in? In what document? Is there is a daily report or daily log?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: It would have to be in the duty officer's log and in the report sent to the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just one more -- if -- Madam Registrar, could you please move to page 12, please, on -- in the English, and B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I would like to ask one or more questions. In the entry it reads: "R-platoon." What does R stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] R-platoon stands for reserve platoon. Those were not active servicemen but reservists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they were not among your three platoons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were part of the 4th Sibenik Company, but they were not active servicemen. They were reserve servicemen. For the purposes of the action itself, some of the men were mobilized.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you said the 4th Company, Sibenik, had three platoons. Did you include the reserve platoons, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now was the R-platoon in Drnis, was that one of the platoons which was directly under your command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the command of Commander Mrkota, not me. I did not have platoons under my command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it becomes less and less clear to me. Ms. Mahindaratne, could you please try to clarify. It's not clear to me what an R-platoon is and was attached to the 4th Company but not military police then or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. The witness's testimony, as I understood, was that the three platoons were within the 4th Company, Sibenik, military police while the witness was the head of the crime military police section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say platoons of military police but not crime police. Let's just -- is that how we have to understood -- there were platoons of the military police but not of the crime section of the military police. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so. Because the service of the military crime police belonged to that company, not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you sent two of your people of the crime police to the platoon in Drnis, which was a military police platoon but not part of the crime police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Only two men from the military crime service went there, because the total service numbered eight men, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Just on that one last clarification, Mr. Simic, when you said the total service number was eight men, not more than that, those eight men were the members of the crime military police section within the 4th Company, Sibenik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we have on the screen one last question on this document, Mr. Simic. At 1150, and this is for the date -- the date on the English document comes from the previous page. And even the B/C/S. There is a record: "The 72nd Military Police Battalion duty officer informed regarding a command of General Cermak that members of UNCRO have complete freedom of movement." Do you know, Mr. Simic, as to how the freedom of movement of UNCRO -- or what role did the 4th Company, Sibenik, play in the control of the movement of UNCRO, UNCRO -- members of UNCRO. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I move this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, before we -- you started asking specific questions, did you not yet tender this document into evidence and was it not yet --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just -- it is possible I may have made a mistake there. If Madam Registrar has a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, let's see ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just -- I will search for the word "admitted."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I have made a mistake. It has been confirmed that it was tendered, P973. My apologies. My apologies, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, may I have document D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, it may be my lack of mastering the English language, but perhaps the parties could assist me in the entry we just read. It says: "Duty officer informed regarding a command of General Cermak ..." Is that the same as an order or is that -- I don't know whether the native speakers could help me out. Whether a command is -- yes. I mean native speakers in -- in the original language rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm a native speaker, Your Honour, but I defer to Mr. Kay on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay's knowledge of the -- of B/C/S is now tested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Was Your Honour asking for any illumination on the matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A command from what -- is that an order or is it a -- a command. As I said, it may be my lack of knowledge --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It exists as a command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It exists as a command. Then I will look at my Webster's. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Madam Registrar, may I have D737, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I'm going to show you a document that you saw last night and this morning, and I appreciate it you would not, in the normal course of business, be familiar with this document. This is a document already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Madam Registrar, if could you move to page 9. And that's in B/C/S 0556. Page 9 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You examined that report which has -- which is included there for the 4th Company, Sibenik. And I'd like you to look at a particular paragraph there. In the English, it's the fourth line from the bottom, which starts with: "Second platoon of the military police that has a total of 33 military policemen." Mr. Simic, do you note that -- in the B/C/S, it's about the seventh line from the bottom, about eighth line. It says: "Second platoon of the military police that has a total of 33 military policemen has been relocated to the liberated city of Drnis. First platoon of the VP and their 24 military policemen have been relocated to Kistanje. Focus tasks were the security of the vital objects and road communications." And then it goes on to describe what their tasks were. Now, you just testified that you sent two men -- two members of the military crime police within your section to Drnis. Likewise, did you also send members of the military crime police to Kistanje, to be attached to the platoon that was sent there?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't, because, automatically I would have endangered the functioning of the service in Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Why do you say that? Can you explain that answer. What do you mean by endangering the functioning of Sibenik -- functioning of the service in Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: If I were to halve the service, according to the AORs and according to the duties within the company itself, I would not have been able to cover all the tasks that I had to make sure were carried out because of the shortage of men. I would have compromised the activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So if any criminal activity were to be investigated which came within the jurisdiction of the military police, which section of the 4th Company, Sibenik, would have had to carry out that activity?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: The military police crime service.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yeah, my -- my question was: Since did you not send any members of the military crime police section to Kistanje, what would they have -- what have been done if it was required to carry out any criminal investigations with regard to activity in Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Had there been any need for it, it would not have been difficult to send an individual from Sibenik to carry out crime scene investigations, rather than keep him there all the time. It wasn't a problem either to instruct the men in Drnis to go to Kistanje, rather than have permanent staff there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, may I call for document 750, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you examined this document last night and this morning. This is a report issued by you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's a monthly report for the period 25th July to 25th August 1995 for your area of responsibility within the 4th Company, Sibenik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are the contents of this report accurate?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Can I see the next page as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if you could go it page 2. Of the B/C/S also.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the content is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, on page 2, it says right at the top there, second line: "Members of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, 4th Company, crime investigation military police through their operative preventive activities in the period between 25th July and 25th August, 1995, filed one criminal report for crime of heavy obstruction of public traffic safety. And in the above-mentioned period, eight crimes were recorded for which criminal reports will be filed." Now if criminal reports were filed with regard to those other eight crimes, where would that have reflected? Would it have reflected in the monthly report for 25th August to the next period?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether that is obvious in this report but there were eight criminal offences registered for which criminal reports would be filed meaning that criminal investigation had not been finished or that -- that they were civilian persons or if they were civilian persons might have been handed over to the MUP and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So where would one have to look to find out exactly what those eight crimes were, since there is no details in -- given in this report?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: In this report. This report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. My question is, since we -- there is no description of what those eight crimes were, where would -- if one wanted to find out what exactly those crimes were, who the perpetrators were, where is it recorded? Is there some kind of formal documentation process whereby one could gather that evidence?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I said that not perhaps all the eight had been processed and perhaps a report was sent subsequently on the commission of these criminal offences. I'm not quite sure what the case was in this particular instance, but the battalion [Realtime transcript read in error "platoon"] should be -- should have such records.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P974.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. The interpreter said battalion not platoon should have such records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, Ms. Mahindaratne. I was puzzled listening to the French channel what the English interpreters would have to tell us. I have now seen it on the screen. P974 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: On the same document, if you could move to page 4 of the same document, page 4 in English. And with B/C/S, it's the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, can you explain to us what those statistics indicate for the month of August. It -- it says reported crimes. Total crimes, 1 -- sorry. Total crimes, 8, it says. And then there is a breakdown: With unknown perpetrators, 3; number of crimes where the perpetrators are identified by the submitter of the report, 2. Number of crimes where the perpetrator was caught in the act, 3. Number of crimes where the perpetrator was discovered at a later stage, 2. And crimes discovered -- percentage of crimes discovered at later stage as compared to known perpetrators, 66.6 per cent; total solved crimes, 7; and percentage of solved crimes as compared to total of crimes, 87.5; and remain unsolved, 1. Now, according to this table, there are a total of seven crimes have been solved, but we see only one criminal report filed, no other details. Are you able to explain to Court what this chart indicates?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: This is the total of reported criminal offences, and later, the action taken to solve them. This is what this table shows.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question was: The seven -- of the seven solved crimes, there is only a reference to one criminal report being filed. What about the balance six?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you're apparently referring the witness to an entry which I have difficulties to find.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. It's on the chart --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And there is under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which column?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's eighth column, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There I read: Total of solved crimes, 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. There we have seven solved crimes. And now somewhere else it reads only one report filed is --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The report filed was at the beginning of the report, Mr. President. I already addressed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not to be found in here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's clear it me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, could you explain to Court, we have seen right at the beginning of this monthly report you referred to one criminal report filed. But according to this chart, it says seven crimes have been solved. Now what about the balance six, were those crimes solved, they were discharged or were criminal reports filed? How would one be able to gather that information?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you could find it in the MUP. Perhaps they were solved by the MUP. Perhaps they were solved by the military police of the 71st Battalion. Maybe it is in their records.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next page, there's another table.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if you could move.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There it is reported that one criminal report was submitted against one soldier for the period August 1995. Is that a reference to the criminal report which -- referred to at the beginning of this report, the first page of this report, where it was mentioned that one criminal report was filed for the crime of heavy obstruction of public traffic safety. Is that one and the same?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Probably. It says the reported criminal offences and the structure of reported persons. In this case, we have one criminal file -- report filed and one person.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, may I have document 3032, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, this is a report issued by you for the month of September on the activities of the crime military police of the 4th Sibenik Company. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. From the -- from the 25th of August to the 25th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could move to the next page, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You examined this report last night and this morning. Are the contents of this report accurate?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I could ask you a question with regard to the first report also. Now, whom do you submit these monthly reports to?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: To the 72nd Battalion, the criminal police, to Mr. Milas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if we remain on page 2 of both the versions. According to this report it says: "4th Company military police members filed four criminal reports for the following crimes, including crime of endangering public traffic, crime of grievous bodily harm, crime of theft of a weapon or a piece of combat equipment, and crime of taking a motor vehicle." It goes on to say, next paragraph: "In the aforementioned period, as a result of responding to reported crimes and regularly patrolling the places where many people as well as HV members gather, the Sibenik military crime police officials filed 33 reports on the violation of military discipline." Now, can you explain to Court, Mr. Simic, what the difference is. There is a reference to criminal reports, four criminal reports being filed against members of the HV and then 33 reports on the violation of military discipline. What kind of crimes would have been -- I'm sorry, the criminal reports, the crimes are described. What kind of acts were caught up in the reports related to violation of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Criminal reports referred to criminal offences committed, and the 33 violations on military discipline is violations, breaches of discipline, committed by members of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if persons were apprehended or just proven that they were found to be looting, what type of reports would be filed? Criminal reports or reports relating to breach of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Criminal reports would be filed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit number P975.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P975 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, may I have document 2440, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I appreciate this is not a document issued by you but it's a document relating to the 4th Company, Sibenik, criminal military police. It's dated 21/9/1995 and it says: "Report regarding acts of criminal military police member in the newly liberated area of Drnis." And it reads that: "There were no criminal reports filed against the Croatian army members in the Drnis area in the aforementioned period. There were 14 disciplinary reports filed against the Croatian army members." And paragraph three says: "The following items were taken from the Croatian army members for which they were issued with the receipt on temporary confiscation of property." And then it gives a list of documents which includes 19 pieces of TV sets and so many domestic appliances and electronic goods. Now, can you explain as to why there are no criminal reports or any type of reports raised in relation to the -- the goods that have been confiscated from the possession of the members of the HV?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember and to the extent that I am familiar with this, all these items were confiscated at a local check-point. What happened with the members, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You just said that -- I asked you a question when it came to looting what type of reports would be filed, whether it's criminal report or reports on breach of military discipline, and you said criminal reports. Now, are you able to offer an explanation as to why no reports have been filed in relation to the -- to the -- this property?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: It is item 5 that provides you with a solution, with an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Items 5 says: "The criminal military police members conducted no independent on-site investigations. They conducted seven on-site investigations in cooperation with the Ministry of Interior members, while five of them were carried out in the presence of an investigating judge." Now, how does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, how does that paragraph explain the absence of there being no criminal reports or any type of reports being filed in relation to this number of property being taken?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: All these items which were confiscated at the check-points when not -- the perpetrators were not caught red-handed stealing them. They were caught having them. Nobody said that they went into a house and looted it. They just had them. That is why no on-site investigations were undertaken for such -- in respect of such items.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So is it the position, then, Mr. Simic, that the crime military police did not charge or file any reports or conduct any investigation in relation to members of the HV who were found having in their possession looted goods, simply because they were not seen looting?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I assume that that is correct. Simply, no one had seen it, and no one was sent to the scene of the event. So no patrols were sent out to the scene nor were they able to find anyone in -- catch anyone in the commission of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was that the general practice in the -- amongst the crime military police of the 72 Military Police Battalion, that if a member of the HV was not caught in the act, there would be no investigation as to whether he had, in fact, perpetrated the particular crime or not?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was the practice, but we needed some concrete material evidence in order to be able to do something. They could all say and they did say at those times, I found it here, I found it there, and that was what we had to grapple with. They would be punished because reports would be sent to the different units, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So when you say that the reports would be sent to the different units, you're talking about as a report of a disciplinary breach, not a criminal report?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I only suppose that they sent reports because I had no insight with the work, into the work of that particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, what were the -- now, you were the head of the crime military police of the 4th Company, Sibenik. What were the instructions that you had received from your superior command as to how to deal with perpetrators who were found looting or who were found with -- in possession of looted goods who were members of the HV?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: According to the rules of procedure of the crime police, crime military police, such people would be brought before the investigating judge. The military investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Apart from the rules, did you have any instructions as to how to deal with the situation after the liberation of the territory from your superior command?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P976.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P976 is admitted into evidence. Could I ask a few questions in relation to this. You have dealt with the documents, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Simic, we see a list of close to 100 items that were taken from Croatian army members, and they were issued with a receipt of temporary confiscation of property. Now what happened with these TV sets, for example? Did you store them, or were they left in the hands of those who had been found in possession of these objects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that those items were taken away, seized and stored in storehouses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tell me where these objects were stored, including the three tractors and five vehicles. You -- where were they stored, since they were seized, from what I understand, in Drnis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were probably sent to barracks for safe custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was probably -- do you know whether they were sent to barracks? And, if so, what barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no supervision over such matters so that I am unable to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes I do know things even if I do not supervise what happened. Do you know or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you exclude for the possibility that these items were left in the hands of those who were found in possession of these objects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot rule out that possibility, because receipts were issued for goods seized. At least that was the practice then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did that mean, that receipts were issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That meant that a certain person had taken a certain item, a TV set, and its brand, its type would be indicated and such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's then put on a piece of paper. And then what happened -- you talked about the practice at the time. What then happened with the TV set once it had been put on paper what brand it was ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't call it a piece of paper. It was a receipt which had its number, its seal and a signature. It was a valid document. Namely, if the owner appeared at any point or if it was established that it had been the object of a criminal offence, then that paper would be invoked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I asked you, as a matter of fact, what happened with a TV set once this was put on paper. Was it kept, was it held in custody by the person with whom it was found or ... and did he have to return it once an owner would show up? Is that what happened or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These objects were seized from unknown perpetrators against a receipt for seized objects. Namely, one could not hold a receipt and hold on to an item. So that the items, I suppose, were sent to barracks and other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You suppose that. But you do not know, if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you say they were seized from unknown perpetrators. But the persons from which they were seized were known, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only said in this particular incident, by way of example, the perpetrators are unknown. But these receipts did specify the object taken and from whom it was taken, by name and surname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Why were they taken from these persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a soldier cannot go to war holding a TV set under his arm. It is to be supposed that it is not his property. He must have taken it from somewhere or someone must have been given to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're telling us that all these TV sets and video players, that you assumed that they did not belong to the soldiers who were found in possession of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you ever interview those persons known by name of which you thought they were in the possession of items that were not owned by them? Did you go and interview them; did you give any follow-up to the seizure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not come into contact with these persons because this took place in the area of Drnis; I wasn't there. Kresmir Balkas [phoen], lieutenant, was in charge of that area, not I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But this is a report to the criminal military police in Sibenik. Did you never ask what -- whether they gave it any follow-up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were probably attempts at finding the rightful owner in order to return these items to him or her. That was the objective of all this activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever receive reports about, for example, these 100 items, whether any of these items was returned to the rightful owner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... any reports on follow-up, apart from what you said was the purpose of all it, but did you ever receive reports on whether that was -- purpose was ever achieved by further investigation, by identifying owners, by ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have such information. That sort of feedback is something I did not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said these people would be punished since it was reported to -- I think you said their commanders. Do you have any information about people being punished, specific information, about people being punished for having been found in the possession of items, you say, you had to assume they were not theirs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kresmir Balkas could have known about this because this was his responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you whether you have any specific knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not. I don't have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm looking at the clock. Five minutes too late. I should look at the clock earlier. Could we ask -- first of all, Mr. Simic, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony you have given already, or the testimony still to be given. Yes, and I take it that you want to see that we provide the witness with a copy of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually I was going to just advise the Court that we provided it to him in the last break. I don't know if you wish that he retrain it overnight or -- but I leave it to Your Honour to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Simic, I do understand that you were provided with a copy of the statement that you gave to the Defence. Would you please carefully read it, if have you not done yet already, and bring it tomorrow. I again instruct you, you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether given already or still to be given, nor about the statement. You should refrain from communicating with anyone about these matters. Then, Mr. Usher, could you please -- and we'd like to see you back tomorrow, I think in the afternoon, Madam Registrar. Yes, would you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you give us an estimate on the time you'd still need? I see that you are two off from the end of your list. Is that 2440 is, there are two others to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would have about another half an hour of examination left. But I didn't understand exactly what you meant when you said I'm two off --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I see on your exhibit list, I think the last document you were dealing with was 2440 which is on my list but that might not be the last one --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. That's what I was dealing with, 2440, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On my list there were two still following, but you may not follow that order. Let's -- you need half an hour. Could I inquire with the Defence how much time Defence counsel would need. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm going to be less than two hours. I will review it again tonight. In light of a 92 ter from the Defence side, I think I might be able to shorten that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Half an hour as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That brings us to three hours all together. And Ms. Mahindaratne, half an hour for you, that makes it three and a half hours. That fits into one session. The parties are urged to use their time in such a way that we can conclude the testimony of this witness tomorrow. And if you say you'd need another half an hour, I think -- yes. Initial estimate was two hours. You've used -- you asked for one more hour. We said we wouldn't stop you, but we would look at how it would develop. You have used now 2 hours 13 minutes. Half an hour is granted and -- but we'll keep you to that rather strictly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, may I just -- for what it's worth, it is clear from the estimates given by the Defence that we would be able to conclude tomorrow, but the witness did indicate that he wished to leave tomorrow for medical reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To leave tomorrow -- tomorrow evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Tomorrow night, Mr. President. It doesn't interfere with the court time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is another reason why we should try to conclude tomorrow. We adjourn, and we will resume tomorrow, the 10th of October, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
